newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British Business - May 22.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British Business - May 22.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
-- SKETCHLEY SET FOR SHAKE-UP

Richard Meyers, finance director for Sketchley, is to leave following the discovery of accountancy deficiencies, in the retail division, by the group's auditors, which involve incorrect stock valuations and under providing for the cost of the company's shop closure programme. There is no accusation of fraud or personal gain. Major shareholders say they may demand further board departures.
-- BASS PLANS MORE HOTEL ACQUISITIONS IN EUROPE

Ian Prosser, chairman of Bass, the brewing and leisure group, says the group will make further hotel acquisitions, particularly in Europe. This comes as Bass announce interim pre- tax profits of ten per cent. Bass plans to make its Holiday Inn chain more of a global brand and recognises that it is considerably weaker in Europe than in the US. Analysts believe Prosser will reconsider buying the William Hill betting chain from Brent Walker and merge it with Bass's Coral Racing.
-- CAMMELL LAIRD HOPES TO RAISE FOUR MILLION STG WITH FLOAT

Birkenhead ship repair and conversion business Cammell Laird is planning to float on the Stock Exchange this summer. The company plans to raise four million stg in an institutional placing through broker Beeson Gregory that will value it at 20 million stg. The float will make Cammell Laird Britain's first quoted ship repair and conversion yard.
THE TIMES
-- SIGNET PLANS 510 MILLION STG SHAKE-UP

The jewelry group which was previously known as Ratners, Signet, has announced its recovery with a 510 million stg restructuring, which will leave ordinary shareholders with 17.5 per cent of the group. The plan needs approval by a 75 per cent majority of all classes of shareholders at a series of meetings next month. Signet's nine classes of shares will be rolled into one, eliminating US and UK preference shares with a face value of 345 million stg and unpaid dividends totalling 165 million stg.
-- NU GIVES 25 PENCE EXTRA DISCOUNT TO MEMBERS

Life insurer Norwich Union announced a 25 pence discount for members in the UK wishing to top up their windfall holdings. The increase boosts the average payout to members by a third to 1,500 stg. The insurer is planning to distribute three billion stg of free share to members when it floats next month and has failed to contact nearly 300,000 members. Handouts to members could increase due to speculation of a pre-floatation takeover bid from Australian life insurer AMP.
-- UNIONS IN TALKS WITH BLAIR'S TEAM

TUC General Secretary John Monks has revealed that union leaders have opened talks with the Government. He said trade union leaders have begun a programme of meetings with senior ministers. He told the TUC's governing executive committee that there is a different mood in Whitehall and Westminster. Monks met the Prime Minister Tony Blair on Tuesday for a discussion on employment issues, the social chapter, allowing unions back into the GCHQ and a statutory minimum wage.
THE GUARDIAN
-- CRACKS AT PILKINGTON AS CHIEF GOES WITH ONE MILLION STG PAYOFF

Peter Leverton, chief executive of Pilkington, the glass group, has been dismissed for failing to cut costs fast enough. He will be given one million stg in compensation and share option profits. Leverton had a two-year rolling contract and was one year into a three-year cost cutting plan. Pressure has been put on the group due to falling European glass prices and a strong pound.
-- RAILTRACK UNDER THE COSH

John Prescott, the deputy prime minister, is considering publishing a White Paper to tighten regulation of the railways to make them more publicly accountable. This comes as regulator John Swift said the company's delivery on its investment plans had been disappointing. He said that a backlog of expenditure on network assets, stations and depots had built up which must be "eradicated" by Railtrack immediately.
-- US INSURERS FIGHT BEING DRAGGED INTO TOBACCO PAYOUT

The US insurance industry has said it will fight any attempt to force its members to contribute towards a 350 billion dollar settlement which is being negotiated between cigarette companies and those suing them for damages. A spokesman for the American Insurance Association said the industry is not part of the settlement negotiations. He said any deal by tobacco companies to reach an agreement with the state and individual litigants would need Congressional approval.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- GEORGE THOUGHT OF QUITTING OVER BANK REFORMS

Governor of the Bank of England, Eddie George, has announced that he considered resigning his position in protest at the removal of his powers of banking supervision by Chancellor Gordon Brown. He has not spoken at length about the lack of the Government's consultation with the Treasury. The removal of the Bank's powers is seen as a rebuke from the Government for its perceived failure to prevent the collapse of BCCI and Barings.
-- F1 TEAM THREATEN FLOAT DELAY

A dispute over the size of the share stake allocated to constructors has lead to leaders of Grand Prix teams threatening to delay the flotation of the Formula One motor racing business until the autumn. The teams are unhappy about proposals drawn up by US investment bank Salomom Brothers over the ten per cent stake in the floated company to be distributed among the constructors. Owner of Formula One, Bernie Ecclestone, is in discussion with top teams, including Williams and McLaren.
-- CELLTECH TRIAL FAILURE SENDS SHARES PLUMMETING

The UK's second biggest company in the biotechnology sector, Celltech, has seen its share price plunge by nearly 50 per cent after the group said its leading project had failed the final stage of clinical trails. The news affected the whole of the biotechnology sector with shares in Scotia, PPL Therapeutics, Cortecs and Cantab falling heavily. Celltech's finance director, Peter Allen, said the news was a severe disappointment. BMC +44-171-377-1742
